output.title: Reference data first, automation second
output.body:
If your business keeps updating the same reference data by hand, that is usually the first workflow to look at before you automate anything downstream. By reference data, I mean the stable inputs your tools depend on: customer names, supplier details, product codes, pricing tiers, approval thresholds, and similar fields. The practical question is simple: where does that data live today, who edits it, and how often does it drift between spreadsheet, email, and software?

If the answer is scattered, or changed by hand every week or so, I would not start with a clever automation. I would first centralize one dataset into a single source of truth, then decide which tools should read from it. That is a bounded next step, and it is often the difference between useful automation and a tidy mess.

Keep the scope small. Pick one reference set, write down the current owner, the update path, and the one downstream process that breaks when the data is stale. Define the baseline before you build anything, including what you want to measure later. Otherwise you end up automating yesterday’s spreadsheet, which is a bold design choice but not a good one.

Human approval still matters for money movement and other high-risk decisions. Before you automate, make sure the reference data has one owner and one update path.
